End
END
n. (rendering Hebrew qēts and 'acharīth, Greek telos)
From Old English ende. The two biblical words divide the sense usefully. Hebrew qēts is a cut-off point, a termination; 'acharīth is the latter end, the outcome of a thing, what it comes to. Greek telos carries both termination and goal — the end of a road being also the purpose of walking it — which is why telos gives English teleology. Scripture's doctrine of the end is almost always this second sense: not merely when a thing stops but what it was for.

Biblical Definition

End in Scripture means outcome and goal more often than mere termination, and the distinction carries most of the doctrine. Ecclesiastes states the principle as a proverb of judgment: “Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit” (Ecc 7:8) — beginnings are cheap and impressive, and only the end shows what a thing was. The Lord Jesus applies this to profession of faith in words that have troubled every shallow assurance: “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13). The verse does not teach that endurance earns salvation; it teaches that endurance is what saving faith does, so that perseverance is the evidence rather than the price. Paul then uses the word in its highest sense, making Christ the goal toward which the whole law was always pointing: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth” (Rom 10:4). Telos here means terminus and purpose together — the law's demands are ended for the believer because they are fulfilled in Christ, and the law's whole design is reached in Him. Peter draws the practical conclusion for a church under pressure, and it is notably sober rather than feverish: “But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer” (1Pe 4:7). Scripture's expectation of the end never produces excitement or withdrawal; it produces sobriety, watchfulness, and prayer.

Webster 1828 Definition

The extreme point or termination of a thing; the conclusion or issue; the final purpose or design for which a thing exists; and in Scripture the end one must endure unto, and Christ who is the end of the law for righteousness.

expand to see more

END, n. 1. The extreme point of a line, or of any thing that has more length than breadth.

2. The last; the conclusion; the close; termination; as the end of the year.

3. Final determination; issue; result; the latter end, or what a thing comes to at last.

4. Ultimate object or purpose; final cause; that for the sake of which a thing is done. The end of the commandment is charity. 1 Tim. 1.

5. In Scripture, he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Matt. 24. Christ is the end of the law. Rom. 10.

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 7:8 — "Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit."

Matthew 24:13 — "But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved."

Romans 10:4 — "For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth."

1 Peter 4:7 — "But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer."

Modern Corruption

Perseverance is either turned into a condition the believer must meet in his own strength, robbing assurance, or dissolved altogether into a bare once-saved formula which needs no fruit — and the end of all things is made a subject for speculation rather than sobriety.

expand to see more

Mat 24:13 is pulled in two wrong directions. On one side it is read as making salvation conditional upon a stamina the believer must supply, so that assurance becomes impossible and the Christian life is lived under audit. On the other it is emptied by a bare formula which holds that a past decision guarantees a future regardless of any fruit whatever, so that endurance is optional and apostasy proves nothing. The Reformed doctrine avoids both by naming the agent: the perseverance of the saints is grounded in the preservation of God. He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ; my sheep shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. Endurance is therefore certain because God keeps His people, and it is genuinely necessary because it is the way He keeps them — the evidence of regeneration rather than its price, and not a bare formula that can be recited over a life with no fruit at all.

The second corruption concerns the end of all things. Peter's statement that it is at hand is made the occasion for date-setting, chart-making, and a fascination with the sequence of last events that Scripture nowhere encourages — and, at the other extreme, for a withdrawal from ordinary duty on the ground that the world is ending anyway. Peter's own inference is neither: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer, and in the next verse, above all things have fervent charity among yourselves. The dictionary holds the closed canon and the certain return of Christ while declining the novelties of a nineteenth-century prophetic system. The principle to recover is that the nearness of the end is given as a motive to sobriety, prayer, and love — and that a man ready to meet Christ today needs no calendar.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qēts is a cut-off point or termination; 'acharīth is the latter end, the outcome or what a thing comes to. Greek telos means both termination and goal, and sunteleia is the consummation of an age.

expand to see more

Hebrew qēts (H7093) — an end, cut-off point, or limit; from a root meaning to cut off, as the end of days.

Hebrew 'acharīth (H319) — the latter end, outcome, or issue of a thing; oh that they would consider their latter end (Deu 32:29).

Greek telos (G5056) — end, termination, and also goal or purpose; Christ is the end of the law (Rom 10:4), both its terminus and its aim.

Greek sunteleia (G4930) — a completing together, consummation; the end of the world (Mat 28:20), literally the consummation of the age.

Greek hupomenō (G5278) — to remain under, endure, persevere; he that shall endure unto the end (Mat 24:13).

Usage

"Of the end as the test of a thing: better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof (Ecc 7:8)."

"Of Christ as the law's goal: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth (Rom 10:4)."

"Of the sobriety the end requires: the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer (1Pe 4:7)."
